front: Which lobe, when collapsed, silhouettes the right heart border and produces a triangular density with its apex at the hilum on the lateral chest radiograph?
back: Right middle lobe collapse.

front: What are the characteristic location and appearance of asbestos-related pleural plaques on chest radiograph?
back: Bilateral lower-zone posterolateral and diaphragmatic dome plaques arising from the parietal pleura, with holly-leaf calcification.

front: Asbestos-related pleural plaques characteristically arise from which layer of the pleura?
back: The parietal pleura.

front: In thoracic sarcoidosis, what defines Scadding stage 2?
back: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy PLUS parenchymal involvement (stage 1 = nodes alone; stage 3 = parenchyma only; stage 4 = fibrosis).

front: What is a traumatic pneumatocele?
back: A thin-walled cystic space in otherwise normal lung, appearing after blunt chest trauma.

front: Honeycomb destruction at the lung bases favours which diagnosis over congestive heart failure?
back: Pulmonary fibrosis.

front: After seat-belt trauma, what chest radiograph pattern suggests right diaphragmatic injury?
back: Elevated right hemidiaphragm with mediastinal shift to the left.

front: What is the classic clinical-imaging pattern of chronic eosinophilic pneumonia?
back: Months of peripheral non-segmental consolidation with eosinophilia, resolving rapidly on corticosteroids.

front: What radiographic measurements indicate scapholunate dissociation?
back: Scapholunate (SL) gap of 3-4 mm (Terry-Thomas sign) and scapholunate angle >60-70 degrees (normal 30-60 degrees).

front: What is the classic radiographic appearance of osteosarcoma?
back: Metaphyseal lytic lesion with cloud-like osteoid matrix ossification and perpendicular (sunburst) periosteal reaction.

front: On infant hip ultrasound, what alpha and beta angles define a normal (Graf type 1) hip?
back: Alpha angle >60 degrees and beta angle <55 degrees.

front: What is the characteristic bone scintigraphy finding in osteoid osteoma?
back: The double-density sign - intense focal activity within modest diffuse activity (clinical clue: night pain).

front: An adolescent girl has sudden pelvic pain and a MIDLINE pelvic cystic mass. What is the most likely diagnosis, and why is dermoid less likely?
back: Hematometrocolpos (imperforate hymen is the commonest cause); a dermoid cyst is adnexal/lateral rather than midline.

front: In which quadrant of the breast do most breast lesions arise?
back: The upper outer quadrant.

front: An enhancing nasopharyngeal mass widening the pterygopalatine fossa in a young patient suggests which diagnosis?
back: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

front: How many standard views make up a neonatal cranial ultrasound examination?
back: 6 coronal + 5 sagittal (paper key wording); some texts say at least 5 + 5.

front: On which properties of a medium does the speed of ultrasound propagation depend?
back: On the density AND compressibility (stiffness) of the medium.

front: What is the focal spot size in mammography, and what magnification is used in magnification (macro-) mammography?
back: Focal spot 0.3 mm (0.3-0.4); magnification 1.5-2x, also called macroradiography.

front: What is bremsstrahlung radiation, and what is its role in x-ray production at 100 kVp with a tungsten target?
back: Projectile electrons decelerated near tungsten nuclei convert kinetic energy into a continuous x-ray spectrum; it is the dominant interaction producing x-rays at 100 kVp (characteristic radiation only above the 69.5 keV K-edge).

front: How are grid ratio and grid frequency defined?
back: Grid ratio = height of the lead strips / interspace distance; grid frequency = lines per cm.

front: Which renal tumour and systemic lesions characterise von Hippel-Lindau disease, and which fat-containing renal lesion belongs to a different syndrome?
back: Clear cell RCC, hemangioblastomas, pheochromocytoma, renal/pancreatic cysts; angiomyolipoma belongs to tuberous sclerosis.

front: What is the triad of Kartagener syndrome, and what should be assessed later in life?
back: Dextrocardia + situs inversus + sinusitis/nasal polyps (primary ciliary dyskinesia); assess infertility.

front: What is the investigation of choice for pelviureteric junction obstruction?
back: MAG3 diuretic renography (gives split renal function and drainage; RCR iRefer).

front: What contrast agent is used in MRI?
back: A gadolinium chelate.

front: What combination defines Plummer-Vinson (Paterson-Kelly) syndrome?
back: Cervical oesophageal web + iron deficiency anaemia.

front: During a barium swallow, on which view is unilateral pharyngeal palsy assessed?
back: The frontal (AP) view.

front: In which cardiac conditions is hyoscine (anticholinergic) contraindicated?
back: Angina/cardiac ischaemia and tachyarrhythmia.

front: Describe the arterial supply of the left adrenal gland.
back: Superior - left inferior phrenic artery; middle - aorta; inferior - left renal artery.

front: Match the radiation quantities to their units: air kerma, absorbed dose, equivalent dose.
back: Air kerma - gray; absorbed dose - gray; equivalent dose - sievert.

front: Which probe and approach are used for infant cranial ultrasound?
back: A small-footprint sector probe via the anterior fontanelle.

front: What is the commonest non-renal retroperitoneal mass of childhood?
back: Neuroblastoma.

front: Which MRI artifact shows opposing dark and bright bands at fat-water interfaces (e.g. bladder wall on T2), and what is it also called?
back: Chemical shift artifact (India ink / second kind).

front: Where do extra-adrenal paragangliomas occur most commonly?
back: Along the sympathetic chain (organ of Zuckerkandl).

front: What is the investigation of choice for urethral diverticulum?
back: MRI.

front: Among pediatric abdominal malignancies, which most commonly metastasises to lung?
back: Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumour).

front: Define bremsstrahlung.
back: Conversion of projectile electron kinetic energy into electromagnetic radiation.

front: At what vertebral level does the IVC commence?
TOACS: extra-axial lesion on CT brain - diagnosis and main differential?
back: Meningioma; main differential is extradural hematoma.

front: TOACS: A plain CT brain (axial sections) is given for a posterior fossa anomaly station - what is the expected diagnosis?
back: Dandy-Walker malformation.

front: TOACS: A sagittal contrast-enhanced CT of the aorta is shown - what diagnosis is expected?
back: Coarctation of the aorta.

front: TOACS: A right-sided aortic arch is seen on the frontal CXR - what must the answer cover?
back: Report the finding, give the diagnosis, and state the cause.

front: TOACS: CXR shows situs inversus + bronchiectasis + multiple cavities - what is the syndrome and the next investigation?
back: Kartagener syndrome; next investigation is CT PNS (paranasal sinuses).

front: TOACS: Coronal T2 MRI shows a didelphys uterus - in what clinical workup is this station set?
back: Infertility workup.

front: TOACS: A TRUS prostate study is shown - what diagnosis is expected?
back: Prostatic abscess.

front: TOACS: Coronal CT abdomen/pelvis shows gas-forming infection of the kidney and bladder - what diagnoses are expected?
back: Emphysematous pyelonephritis + (emphysematous) cystitis.

front: TOACS: An inguino-scrotal hernia is causing bowel obstruction - which study checks for bowel ischaemia?
back: A contrast study (to check for bowel ischaemia).

front: TOACS: Plain + contrast CT brain is shown in a stroke station - which infarct is expected?
back: Right MCA (middle cerebral artery) infarct.

front: TOACS: X-ray pelvis shows bilateral femoral head AVN - what is the next most appropriate investigation?
back: MRI.

front: TOACS: A coronal CT abdomen is shown in the acute abdomen station - what surgical diagnosis is expected?
back: Perforated appendix.

front: TOACS: Left lower lobe (LLL) consolidation with collapse on CXR - list the supporting signs and their marks.
back: Air bronchogram; silhouette of the left hemidiaphragm and descending aorta (1 mark each).

front: TOACS: X-ray KUB shows faecal loading, a deformed pelvis, fused ilium and a non-visualised sacrum - diagnosis and next investigation?
back: Sacral agenesis type IV; next investigation is MRI.

front: TOACS: Summarise the CT sinogram/fistulogram station (marks, contrast, non-ionising alternative).
back: Sinogram/fistulogram description carries 3 marks + procedure/technique 5 marks; contrast is LOCM; the non-ionising alternative is an MR sinogram.

front: TOACS: A T-tube cholangiogram shows a filling defect in the duct - what is the finding/diagnosis?
back: Worm (ascariasis).

front: TOACS: CT brain shows intraparenchymal haematoma with intraventricular extension, likely a ruptured aneurysm - what is the next investigation?
back: CT angiography or four-vessel DSA.

front: TOACS: CT lumbosacral spine sagittal/axial images at L2 (bone window) are shown - what bone lesion diagnosis is expected?
back: Aneurysmal bone cyst.

front: TOACS: A mammogram shows a highly suspicious lesion - which BI-RADS category is expected?
back: BI-RADS 5.

front: TOACS: AP and lateral views show a lesion of the right hemimandible - what diagnosis is expected?
back: Ameloblastoma of the right hemimandible.

front: TOACS anatomy: On a brain MRV, which venous structures must you be able to name?
back: Superior sagittal sinus; transverse sinus; vein of Labbe; sigmoid sinus; jugular bulb; occipital/vertebral venous plexus.

front: TOACS anatomy: Which veins should you identify on a SVC venogram?
back: Right subclavian; right brachiocephalic; SVC; azygos; hemiazygos veins.

front: TOACS anatomy: Which foramina and related structures should you identify on an axial skull-base CT (bone window)?
back: Foramen ovale; foramen spinosum; foramen lacerum; sphenoid sinus; inferior orbital fissure.

front: TOACS physics: Name the ultrasound artifacts you may be asked to identify.
back: Reverberation; comet tail; ring down; mirror image.

front: TOACS anatomy: On HRCT of the temporal bone, which inner-ear/middle-ear structures should you identify?
back: Posterior SCC; anterior SCC; vestibule; facial nerve canal; mastoid antrum.

front: TOACS physics: Define optical density (with formula) and the terms: grid, grid cutoff, grid ratio, grid types, air gap, ALARA, HVL.
back: Optical density = log10 of the incident-to-transmitted light ratio; grid = anti-scatter grid; grid cutoff = loss of primary transmission with incorrect grid use; grid ratio = strip height / interspace; grid types (linear/crossed, focused/parallel); air gap technique; ALARA = as low as reasonably achievable; HVL = half-value layer.

front: TOACS: Identify these MRI coils - which types are commonly shown?
back: Endorectal coil; breast coil; extremity coil; body phased-array coil.

front: TOACS nuclear medicine: For a Meckel's scan, name the tracer, the finding/diagnosis, and one other example of this tracer's use.
back: Tracer: Tc-99m pertechnetate; finding/diagnosis: Meckel's diverticulum (ectopic gastric mucosa); other example: any other pertechnetate use (e.g. gastric mucosa/thyroid imaging).

front: TOACS physics: Name the views of the FAST scan and state what eFAST adds.
back: Name the FAST views (perihepatic, perisplenic, pelvic, pericardial); eFAST adds the thoracic views to FAST.

front: TOACS physics: what is the minimum lead-equivalent thickness of a protective apron?
back: At least 0.5 mm lead equivalent.

front: TOACS: What are the indications and contraindications of X-ray flexion-extension views?
back: Indications: demonstration of abnormal segmental motion/instability (e.g. suspected ligamentous injury on delayed films, rheumatoid arthritis, spondylolisthesis). Contraindications: acute unstable trauma/injury not yet excluded, and uncooperative patients.

front: TOACS: For AP internal and external rotation views of the shoulder, how is centring performed?
back: Centre on the shoulder (glenohumeral) joint, with the arm in internal rotation for one exposure and external rotation for the other.

front: TOACS: Describe the Rosenberg view - centring and patient position relative to the detector.
back: A weight-bearing knee view: the patient stands with the knee flexed against the detector; centred on the knee joint (assesses joint space under load).

front: TOACS: MRI shows T2/T1 post-contrast ring-enhancing lesions with mild vasogenic oedema - diagnosis?
back: Tuberculoma.

front: TOACS: HRCT temporal bone shows bilateral mastoiditis with soft tissue in the internal and external acoustic meatus - what diagnosis is suspected?
back: Mastoiditis with cholesteatoma.

front: TOACS: The fibula shows a permeative lesion with periosteal reaction and soft tissue thickening - give the differential.
back: Osteosarcoma vs osteomyelitis.

front: TOACS: MRI hip in a renal transplant patient - what complication is shown?
back: Bilateral femoral head avascular necrosis (AVN).

front: TOACS: Knee X-ray shows sclerosis with irregular lateral tibial plateau margins - classify the fracture.
back: Schatzker type 2 fracture (as written 'shatzik type 2').

front: TOACS: Rapid-fire diagnoses - CT abdomen renal mass; MRI pelvis enlarged cystic kidneys; CXR mediastinal vascular lesion; CXR air outlining the mediastinum. Name each.
back: Wilms tumour; polycystic kidney disease; pulmonary arterial aneurysm; pneumomediastinum.

front: TOACS: HRCT shows a branching nodule with left pleural effusion - diagnosis?
back: Tuberculosis.

front: TOACS: (a) MRCP filling defects in the distal CBD; (b) CT tissue encircling the D2 vs an ulcer crater; (c) CT caecal thickening. Give the diagnoses.
back: (a) Choledocholithiasis; (b) annular pancreas vs peptic ulcer at D2; (c) colon cancer vs appendicitis.

front: TOACS: (a) Mammogram with a suspicious lesion - category? (b) Acute scrotum ultrasound - diagnosis? (c) Water view - finding?
back: (a) BI-RADS 4/5 lesion; (b) right testicular torsion; (c) bilateral maxillary sinusitis on water view.

back: Plumbicon or vidicon pickup tubes.

front: TOACS physics: A CT phantom image is given showing circular bands centred on the gantry - which artifact is this?
back: Ring artifact.

back: At least 0.5 mm lead equivalent.

front: TOACS: List typical focal spot sizes across modalities - mammography, macroradiography, general radiology, fluoroscopy.
back: Mammography 0.3 mm; macroradiography 0.1-0.76 mm; general radiology 1.0-1.2 mm; fluoroscopy ~0.6 mm.

front: TOACS: Describe TRUS prostate biopsy - patient position and the sextant protocol.
back: Position and sextant protocol: samples are taken of the peripheral zone (higher diagnostic yield) from base through middle to apex, bilaterally (six cores).

front: TOACS physics: Compare continuous vs pulsed Doppler; define steering angle, Doppler angle and patient position.
back: Continuous wave: transmits and receives continuously (no range resolution); pulsed wave: gated sample volume with range resolution. Steering angle and Doppler angle (keep <60 degrees) are set relative to the vessel; patient position optimises the insonation angle.

front: TOACS: Ankle mortise view - positioning, centring, and indication.
back: Positioning: leg internally rotated (typically 15-20 degrees) with the ankle in the mortise profile; centring: midway between the malleoli; indication: assessment of the ankle mortise/tibial plafond and medial clear space.

back: Barium with methylcellulose; tube tip placed distal duodenum/proximal jejunum; uses: mucosal detail, tumours and inflammatory disease of the small bowel.

front: TOACS: Non-contrast CT brain shows a hyperdense right MCA cistern and right temporal lobe changes - diagnosis?
back: Subarachnoid + intracerebral haemorrhage (hyperdense MCA sign).

front: TOACS: A large globular heart with narrow pedicle and clear lung fields - diagnosis?
back: Pericardial effusion (water-bottle heart).

front: TOACS: ERCP shows a hyperdense focus in the CBD - diagnosis?
back: Choledocholithiasis.

front: TOACS: IVU 10-min film shows dilated pelvicalyceal systems with medially tilted pelvises - diagnosis?
back: Horseshoe kidney.

front: TOACS: X-ray pelvimetry - identify line A and line B, and name alternative modalities.
back: Line A = pelvic inlet; line B = true conjugate; alternatives: CT pelvimetry and MRI pelvimetry.

front: TOACS: Lateral elbow radiograph shows elevation of BOTH anterior and posterior fat pads - what does this signify and which fracture is usual?
back: It signifies an underlying fracture - most commonly radial neck/medial neck (as written).

front: TOACS: A child's chest X-ray shows enlarged bulbous distal ribs - what is this sign and which additional radiographs are indicated?
back: Ricketic rosary (rickets); also image the wrists and knees.

front: TOACS: Cranio-caudal mammogram shows a low-density, well-defined lesion in the inner quadrant - diagnosis?
back: Lipoma.

front: TOACS: A pregnant patient with altered consciousness has bilateral thalamic infarcts - what venous diagnosis is expected?
back: Internal cerebral vein thrombosis (deep cerebral venous thrombosis).

front: TOACS nuclear medicine: state the half-lives of I-123, I-131, Tl-201 and F-18.
TOACS radiation protection: State the annual radiographer dose limit and typical doses for CT brain, CT abdomen and chest radiograph.
back: Occupational limit 20 mSv/year (ICRP); CT brain 1-2 mSv; CT abdomen 8 mSv; chest radiograph ~0.02 mSv.

front: TOACS physics: Identify these artefacts - patient movement blur; metal-related radial lines; gantry-centred rings; India-ink bands.
back: Motion; streak; ring; India ink (chemical shift) artefacts.

front: TOACS physics: What standard gadolinium dose is given to an 80 kg patient, and what adverse effects should be stated?
back: Standard single dose 0.1 mmol/kg = 8 mmol for 80 kg; adverse effects of gadolinium-based contrast (e.g. hypersensitivity, NSF) (answers to verify).

front: TOACS station 1A: CT right petrous temporal bone (bone window, two axial + two coronal reformats) - which structures must you identify?
back: Internal auditory canal (IAC); cochlea; facial canal; and the labelled temporal bone structures.

front: State the exact half-lives of I-123, I-131, Tl-201 and F-18.
Give typical doses: chest radiograph, CT brain, CT abdomen, and the occupational annual limit.
back: Chest radiograph 0.02 mSv; CT brain 1-2 mSv; CT abdomen 8 mSv; occupational limit 20 mSv/y averaged over 5 years (ICRP).

front: An 80 kg patient needs gadolinium at 0.1 mmol/kg. How many mmol and how many mL of a 0.5 mmol/mL agent?
back: 8 mmol = ~16 mL of a 0.5 mmol/mL agent.

front: What liver attenuation values are normal on non-contrast CT, what threshold indicates moderate steatosis, and how does a steatotic liver compare with the spleen?
back: Normal ~50-65 HU; <40-45 HU indicates moderate hepatic steatosis; steatotic liver measures lower than the spleen (LAI = liver-minus-spleen HU concept).

front: Summarise the published Graf hip-ultrasound classification (alpha/beta angles).
back: I: alpha >=60 (Ia beta <=55, Ib beta >55); IIa+/IIa-: alpha 50-59; IIb: 50-59 after 12 weeks; IIc: 43-49 with beta <=77; IId: 43-49 with beta >77 (decentering); IIIa/b: alpha <43, cartilage shifted superiorly; IV: alpha <43, cartilage shifted inferiorly. (The Feb 2025 paper prints rows 2c/2d differently - see disputed.md.)

front: TOACS labelling: On a shoulder MRI, name the labelled structures.
back: Acromion process; supraspinatus muscle and tendon; trapezius; surgical neck of humerus; greater tubercle; anatomical neck; deltoid.

front: TOACS labelling: On axial skull-base CT, identify the pterygomaxillary/PPF region and related foramina.
back: Pterygomaxillary fissure/pterygopalatine fossa; sphenopalatine foramen; foramen rotundum; internal auditory canal (companion image also shows: foramen ovale, spinosum, lacerum, carotid canal, clivus, sigmoid sinus, zygomatic arch, nasal septum).

front: TOACS labelling: List the temporal bone landmarks identifiable on axial CT station images.
back: Cochlea (basal/apical turns, promontory, cochlear aqueduct); IAC; vestibule; vestibular aqueduct; lateral/posterior/superior SCC + ampulla; facial nerve (labyrinthine segment, geniculate ganglion); malleus head/short process; Prussak space; incus; scutum; Koerner septum; singular canal; stapes; pyramidal eminence & stapedius; round window; mastoid antrum/air cells; squamous temporal bone; carotid canal.

front: TOACS labelling: At the suprasellar cistern level on axial CT, name the cisterns and midbrain structures.
back: Cisterns: suprasellar, interpeduncular, ambient, quadrigeminal plate, sylvian, crural, interhemispheric fissure, temporal horn; midbrain: red nucleus, substantia nigra, crus cerebri, aqueduct, mamillary bodies, vermis.

front: How many Scadding stages classify sarcoidosis on PA chest radiographs, and what is stage 0?
back: Five stages (0 to IV); stage 0 is a normal chest radiograph (5-15% frequency at presentation).

front: What is Scadding stage I sarcoidosis, how common is it at presentation, and how often does it resolve spontaneously?
back: Hilar or mediastinal nodal enlargement only; 25-65% at presentation; spontaneous resolution in 60-90%.

front: What is Scadding stage II sarcoidosis, and its presentation frequency and spontaneous resolution rate?
back: Nodal enlargement with parenchymal disease; 20-40% at presentation; spontaneous resolution in 40-70%.

front: What is Scadding stage III sarcoidosis, and its presentation frequency and spontaneous resolution rate?
back: Parenchymal disease only; 10-15% at presentation; spontaneous resolution in 10-20%.

front: What is Scadding stage IV sarcoidosis?
back: End-stage lung disease (pulmonary fibrosis); ~5% at presentation; spontaneous resolution 0%.

front: What is Panner disease?
back: Osteochondrosis/osteonecrosis of the capitellum.

front: Which stage of haematoma evolution is T1 hyperintense and T2 hypointense, and when does it occur?
back: Early subacute stage - 3 days to 1 week.

front: Describe the MRI appearances of an early subacute haematoma (3 to 7 days).
back: Intracellular methemoglobin: T1 hyperintense; T2 hypointense; DWI low; ADC low; SWI hypointense.

front: Describe the MRI appearances of a hyperacute haematoma (<12 hours to <1 day).
back: Intracellular oxyhemoglobin: T1 isointense; T2 isointense to hyperintense; DWI high; ADC low; SWI hyperintense with a thin hypointense rim.

front: Describe the MRI appearances of an acute haematoma (1 to 3 days).
back: Intracellular deoxyhemoglobin: T1 isointense to hypointense; T2 hypointense; DWI low; ADC low; SWI hypointense.

front: What happens to T1 and T2 signal in a late subacute haematoma (7 to 14-28 days)?
back: Extracellular methemoglobin: T1 remains hyperintense and T2 gradually increases over the next few weeks.

front: Describe the MRI appearances of a chronic haematoma (>14-28 days).
back: Periphery of intracellular hemosiderin (T1 and T2 hypointense; hypointense rim on SWI) and a centre of extracellular hemichromes (T1 isointense; T2 hyperintense; DWI low; ADC high).

front: On what does the probability of the Compton effect depend?
back: Directly proportional to the electron density of the material; only very weakly dependent on photon energy (relatively constant over 10-600 keV).

front: Which major photon interaction does NOT depend on atomic number (Z)?
back: Compton scatter - unlike the photoelectric effect and pair production.

front: What is the most common detector in direct digital radiography, and how is an indirect flat panel detector constructed?
back: The flat panel detector (FPD); indirect FPD = cesium iodide (CsI) scintillator layer + amorphous silicon (a-Si) photodiode + TFT readout array.

front: What are the advantages of a thermoluminescent dosimeter (TLD) over a film dosimeter?
back: Better accuracy; no need to estimate photon energy; higher dynamic range; reusable (a passive device for personal dose monitoring).

front: What does the modulation transfer function (MTF) describe, and at what MTF value are two systems' limiting spatial frequencies compared?
back: The ability of a detector to retain the contrast (signal amplitude) of an object as spatial frequency increases; comparison at an MTF of 10%.

front: A swelling below and lateral to the pubic tubercle in a female is which hernia?
back: Femoral hernia (FEMORAL: females, below, lateral; INGUINAL: males, above, medial).

front: In which pediatric age group is the AP erect chest view ideal, and what are its drawbacks?
back: Younger cooperative patients (~3-7 years); drawbacks: increased radiation dose to radiosensitive organs and magnification of the heart and mediastinum.

front: What defines isotopes of an element (e.g. of barium)?
back: Same atomic number (same number of protons) but different mass numbers (different numbers of neutrons).

front: Increasing the distance from the x-ray source from 100 cm to 200 cm changes beam intensity how?
back: It decreases to one quarter (inverse square law).

front: What is the effect of increasing tube current (mA) on the image?
back: More photons reach the detector and the signal (image) intensity increases; contrast is not increased.

front: In a V/Q scan, which radiopharmaceuticals are used for the perfusion and ventilation studies?
back: Perfusion: intravenous Tc-99m MAA (particles lodge in pre-capillary arterioles); ventilation: Tc-99m DTPA radioisotope-labeled aerosol.

front: When is double contrast barium preferred over single contrast, and when is single contrast sufficient?
back: Double contrast for better mucosal visualization; single contrast barium enema usually suffices for fistula or postoperative leak evaluation.

front: MCQ trap: What is the best advantage of a double-film/double-emulsion screen system?
back: Higher speed - giving lower patient dose and shorter exposure time (NOT higher spatial resolution).

front: A child with recurrent UTIs has a sacral or lumbar dimple - what does this cutaneous marker suggest?
back: Underlying spinal dysraphism (occult spina bifida or tethered cord).

front: A 2-week-old infant has pulmonary plethora with no cyanosis - what does this indicate?
back: A left-to-right cardiac shunt (ASD, VSD or PDA) - as stated, a VSD.

front: A unilateral radiolucent hemithorax with a small hyperlucent lung, small hila and expiratory air trapping - diagnosis and cause?
back: Swyer-James (MacLeod) syndrome; postinfectious obliterative bronchiolitis.

front: What antecedent infection and age typically precede Swyer-James syndrome, and what is its estimated prevalence?
back: Viral respiratory infection in infancy or early childhood (adenovirus or Mycoplasma pneumoniae); prevalence ~0.01%.

front: A chest x-ray shows a solid-cystic mass with mediastinal shift to the opposite side in a neonate - diagnosis?
back: CCAM (congenital pulmonary airway malformation) type 1.

front: A child has UTI and a back dimple - what is the underlying congenital defect and the functional cause of the UTIs?
back: Occult spinal dysraphism (e.g. diastematomyelia or tethered cord); the UTIs are caused by neurogenic bladder.

front: A distended, trabeculated bladder indicates which type of neurogenic bladder?
back: Lower motor neuron lesion (LMNL) neurogenic bladder.

front: Where is the esophageal opening of the diaphragm located relative to the aortic hiatus and the midline?
back: In the right crus, above, in front of and a little to the left of the aortic hiatus - slightly to the left of the midline.

front: How is aliasing artifact reduced on MRI?
back: Enlarge the field of view; also pre-saturation bands outside the FOV, anti-aliasing software, switching phase/frequency directions, or using a surface coil.

front: What does increasing kVp do to the x-ray beam?
back: It increases x-ray penetration.

front: What is the function of aluminum filtration in the x-ray beam?
back: To remove low-energy photons from the beam.

front: A retrocardiac mass with fluffy borders and an air bronchogram in a child clears on a repeat chest x-ray after 6 weeks - diagnosis?
back: Pneumonia.

front: What artifact does a metallic object produce?
back: Beam-hardening artifact.

front: On CT of a hip joint with a prosthesis, which artifact is expected?
back: Beam hardening.

front: Which syndrome is classically associated with a short fourth metacarpal, and what are other causes?
back: Turner syndrome; also idiopathic, post-infective (osteomyelitis, TB dactylitis), pseudohypoparathyroidism/pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism and post-traumatic shortening.

front: What carotid Doppler criteria indicate a normal ICA or <50% stenosis?
back: ICA PSV <125 cm/sec; ICA/CCA PSV ratio <2.0; ICA EDV <40 cm/sec.

front: What carotid Doppler criteria indicate 50-69% ICA stenosis?
back: ICA PSV 125-230 cm/sec; ICA/CCA PSV ratio 2.0-4.0; ICA EDV 40-100 cm/sec.

front: What carotid Doppler findings indicate >=70% ICA stenosis, near-occlusion and total occlusion?
back: >=70%: ICA PSV >230 cm/sec, ICA/CCA ratio >4, EDV >100 cm/sec; near occlusion: variable velocities with trickle flow; total occlusion: no detectable flow.

front: What is Rigler triad and in which condition is it seen?
back: Pneumobilia + small bowel obstruction/dilation + ectopic calcified gallstone in the small bowel (usually right iliac fossa) - gallstone ileus.

front: What features favour a benign (osteoporotic) over a metastatic vertebral compression fracture?
back: No bony destruction; preserved fatty marrow T1 signal; low-signal fracture-line band on T1/T2; fluid sign; retropulsion (not posterior bulging) of the posterosuperior cortex; no epidural mass; multiple fractures; pedicles not involved.

front: What features favour a pathological (metastatic) vertebral compression fracture?
back: Bony destruction on CT; marrow replacement extending into the pedicles or posterior elements; convex bulging of the posterior vertebral cortex; epidural or paraspinal mass; other vertebral metastases.

front: A well-defined lucent lesion in the breast on mammography is which lesion?
back: A lipoma (as stated).

front: MCQ trap: A lesion seen in the superior aspect on the ML view remains superior on the MLO view - where is it in the breast?
back: Medially in the breast.

front: A spinal lesion in a 17-year-old girl shows increased uptake in the blood pool phase on bone scintigraphy - diagnosis?
back: Aneurysmal bone cyst (as stated).

front: Severe headache with xanthochromia on CSF (subarachnoid haemorrhage) - what is the next investigation?
back: CT angiography.

front: What remains the gold standard for diagnosis and characterization of cerebral vascular abnormalities?
back: Digital subtraction catheter angiography (DSA).

front: Fever, productive cough, continuous headache, basal meningeal enhancement and hydrocephalus on imaging - diagnosis?
back: TB meningitis.

front: What is the most common solid (renal) mass in a 2-month-old infant (as stated)?
back: Mesonephric blastoma (as stated).

front: What is the most common lung metastasis source in the young?
back: Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumour).

front: Which tumours dominate synchronous lung metastasis in men 15-40, adolescents 10-20, and children under 10?
back: 15-40: testicular cancer; 10-20: bone and soft tissue sarcomas; under 10: kidney and soft tissue tumours.

front: Name the most common primaries of pediatric pulmonary metastases, and the most common primary site in adults.
back: Children: rhabdomyosarcoma, osteosarcoma, Wilms tumour, Ewing sarcoma, neuroblastoma; adults: lung cancer.

front: An intermittently symptomatic hyperdense lesion at the 3rd ventricle on unenhanced CT - diagnosis?
back: Colloid cyst.

front: Where do medulloblastomas arise?
back: 94% in the cerebellum; of these, 75% from the vermis, protruding into the fourth ventricle from its roof (superior medullary velum).

front: MCQ trap: In a fourth ventricular tumour, what favours medulloblastoma and what favours ependymoma?
back: Vermian origin and numerous supratentorial deposits favour medulloblastoma; young age and protrusion through the 4th ventricular foramen favour ependymoma (which tends to seed inferiorly).

front: What spinal finding is pathognomonic of achondroplasia, and what limb pattern accompanies it?
back: Progressive decrease in the interpedicular distance in the lumbar spine (narrowest cited at L1); rhizomelic dwarfism (proximal femoral and humeral shortening).

front: What imaging features identify a cerebral mass as intra-axial?
back: Expansion/thickening of the cortex; poorly defined infiltrative margins; no CSF cleft sign; may cross the midline via the corpus callosum; vasogenic oedema (e.g. gliomas, metastases, abscesses, demyelinating plaques).

front: What imaging features identify a cerebral mass as extra-axial?
back: Compression/displacement rather than infiltration of the cortex; well defined; CSF cleft sign; cortical buckling/scalloping of underlying bone; dural tail (meningioma); widened subarachnoid spaces (e.g. meningioma, arachnoid cyst, schwannoma, epidermoid).

front: A CSF-density mass in the temporal region with underlying bone scalloping and no restricted diffusion on DWI - diagnosis?
back: Arachnoid cyst.

front: Which structures run through Guyon's canal, and where is the canal relative to the flexor retinaculum?
back: The ulnar artery and nerve; superficial to the flexor retinaculum (the carpal tunnel itself contains the median nerve and flexor tendons).

front: Which structure occupies the superolateral aspect of the orbit near the eye?
back: The lacrimal gland, within the lacrimal fossa of the frontal bone.

front: Which three forearm injuries are considered unstable fractures?
back: Monteggia, Galeazzi and Essex-Lopresti injuries.

front: What is the terminal branch of the lateral cord of the brachial plexus and its roots?
back: The musculocutaneous nerve (C5, 6, 7); the lateral cord also gives the lateral pectoral nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve.

front: What is the most common cause of multiple calcified pulmonary granulomas?
back: Prior thoracic histoplasmosis (recovered miliary tuberculosis is a rarer cause).

front: With which syndromes/conditions has multicentric giant cell tumour of bone been associated?
back: Phaeochromocytoma-paraganglioma and giant cell tumour syndrome; Paget disease of bone; Gorlin-Goltz syndrome; Jaffe-Campanacci syndrome.

front: What is the most common primary non-cavitating pulmonary mass?
back: Adenocarcinoma.

front: Middle-third anterior vertebral body beaking suggests which syndrome, and which conditions cause lower-third beaking?
back: Middle-third: Morquio syndrome; lower-third: Hurler syndrome, achondroplasia, congenital hypothyroidism, pseudoachondroplasia, Down syndrome and neuromuscular diseases - lymphoma is the 'all except' answer.

front: To which lymph nodes does the cervix drain?
back: Internal iliac nodes (also external iliac and sacral nodes).

front: The ovarian artery is a direct branch of which vessel?
back: The abdominal aorta.

front: A midline abdominal wall defect in a child is which abnormality, and where does gastroschisis lie?
back: Omphalocele; gastroschisis lies to the right of the umbilical cord insertion.

front: Which cranial landmark is formed where four skull bones meet?
back: The pterion.

front: Where does the median arcuate ligament pass relative to the aorta and the celiac artery?
back: In front of the aorta, superior to the origin of the celiac artery.

front: Which fracture is virtually pathognomonic of non-accidental injury, and in what proportion of abused infants is it present?
back: The metaphyseal fracture (bucket-handle or corner fracture); up to 39-50% of abused infants under 18 months.

front: Which fractures are highly specific for non-accidental injury?
back: Posterior rib fractures (not caused by vigorous CPR, may have no overlying bruising), costochondral junction injuries, scapular and sternal fractures.

front: In a baby with encephalomalacic changes from non-accidental injury, which associated finding is stated?
back: A leptomeningeal cyst.

front: Multiple non-communicating cysts in the kidney indicate which condition?
back: Multicystic dysplastic kidney.

front: A cystic area in the renal pelvis causing calyceal dilatation with no contrast filling on IVU is which lesion?
back: A parapelvic cyst.

front: On hysterosalpingography, what does free intraperitoneal spill of contrast indicate?
back: A normal finding - tubal patency.

front: How is a hyperdense lesion in the endometrial cavity confirmed?
back: With sonohysterography.

front: Enlarged ovaries (7 cm) with follicles, a 12 cm cyst, ascites and pleural effusion - diagnosis?
back: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.

front: Which part of the colon does ischemic colitis most commonly affect, and what are the SMA and IMA territories?
back: The left colon; SMA supplies the right colon from cecum to splenic flexure; IMA supplies the left colon from splenic flexure to rectum.

front: Name the colonic watershed areas where low-flow ischemic colitis typically occurs.
back: Splenic flexure (Griffiths point) and rectosigmoid junction (Sudeck point).

front: How is the azygos vein formed, and are its tributaries right- or left-sided?
back: Union of the right ascending lumbar vein and right subcostal veins at ~T12-L2; its tributaries are right-sided (hemiazygos, accessory hemiazygos, right superior intercostal, right posterior intercostal, right superior phrenic, right bronchial, tracheal, esophageal and pericardial veins).

front: How is venous reflux defined on duplex ultrasound?
back: Flow reversal lasting more than 0.5 s; a limit of 1 s is used for the deep venous system (reflux over 1 s is significant).

front: What follow-up does the ESUR advise for testicular microlithiasis?
back: Annual ultrasound until age 55 only if a malignancy risk factor is present (maldescent, orchidopexy, testicular atrophy <12 cc, previous germ cell tumour, family history); with isolated microlithiasis, monthly self-examination.

front: Which forearm muscle is the muscle of the mid-prone position?
back: Brachioradialis.

front: In evacuation proctography (defecography), how is the key reference line drawn?
back: From the tip of the coccyx to the lower border of the pubic ramus.

front: What are the normal anorectal angle and anorectal junction descent on defecography?
back: Anorectal angle ~90-95 degrees at rest and ~135 degrees at evacuation (more obtuse); the anorectal junction descends <3.5 cm, usually to the level of the ischial tuberosities.

front: Describe the defecography technique (contrast, optional opacifications, post-evacuation image).
back: 2-4 x 60 mL of thick barium paste per rectum via a large-bore soft (Miller) catheter; optional small bowel opacification with 500 mL oral barium 30-60 min before; optional vaginal opacification with 5 mL; a post-evacuation straining image looks for retained material or enterocele.

front: Which two muscles does the axillary nerve supply?
back: Teres minor and deltoid.

front: How is CT colonography ideally performed?
back: On an MDCT scanner, supine and prone, with thin collimation (<1 mm slices); colonic distension with pressure-regulated carbon dioxide (preferred) or room air.

front: What is the smallest polyp size CT colonography may detect, and how are residual stool and fluid managed?
back: Polyps 2 mm or larger (significance of <5 mm polyps is questionable); stool/fluid tagged with oral contrast agents such as Gastrografin.

front: How common is bowel perforation after CT colonography and what factors increase the risk?
back: Very rare (0.005%-0.03%); more likely with pre-existing obstructive bowel pathology, stiff rectal catheters, short interval after biopsy at optical colonoscopy, or manual gas insufflation.

front: An overweight 12-year-old shows medial slip of the femoral head (SCFE) - which radiographs assess this?
back: AP and frog-leg lateral radiographs of the pelvis, commonly done bilaterally (many of these injuries are bilateral).

front: In children with intussusception, how often is no lead point found, and what is the stated precipitating cause?
back: No lead point in 90% (attributed to hypertrophic lymphoid tissue / Peyer patches after infection); stated precipitant is acute diarrhea (viral, most commonly adenovirus).

front: How often do adult intussusceptions have a lead point and what is the usual pathology?
back: Up to 90% have a lead point - malignant in the large bowel, benign in the small bowel; GI malignancy accounts for 65% (colorectal carcinoma most common).

front: List the risk factors for peptic ulcer disease.
back: Helicobacter pylori infection; NSAIDs; corticosteroids; severe physiological stress/illness; Zollinger-Ellison syndrome; hypercalcaemia.

front: A hepatic lesion that hyperenhances on the arterial phase and is isointense on delayed imaging in a male on steroid intake is what?
back: Hepatic adenoma.

front: Why is ultrasound the safest and most practical imaging modality in pregnancy?
back: It avoids radiation, is widely available and inexpensive, and provides real-time fetal assessment.

front: Describe the three compartments of the femoral sheath.
back: Two vertical septae divide it into: lateral - common femoral artery; intermediate - common femoral vein; medial - femoral canal (deep inguinal lymph nodes and lymphatic vessels).

front: Which nerve and vessels pierce the thyrohyoid membrane?
back: The internal laryngeal nerve (branch of the superior laryngeal nerve) with the superior laryngeal artery and vein (the pyriform sinus is bounded laterally by the thyroid cartilage and thyrohyoid membrane).

front: What is the arterial supply of the lentiform nucleus?
back: Medial lenticulostriate arteries (from the ACA) and lateral lenticulostriate arteries (from the MCA - the main supply).

front: Where does the superior cerebellar artery arise and what does it supply?
back: From the distal basilar artery just below the posterior cerebral artery; supplies the superior surface of the cerebellar hemispheres down to the great horizontal fissure, the superior vermis, the dentate nucleus and the superior cerebellar peduncle.

front: What supplies the lateral and medial aspects of the medulla?
back: Lateral aspect - posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA); entire medial aspect - anterior spinal artery.

front: Describe the arterial supply of the caudate nucleus (head, superior head/body, tail).
back: Head - recurrent artery of Heubner (branch of A2, sometimes A1, of the ACA); superior head and body - MCA lenticulostriate perforators; tail - anterior choroidal artery.

front: Collapse silencing the right cardiac silhouette (right heart border) indicates collapse of which lobe?
back: Right middle lobe.

front: A hyperdense sinonasal lesion causing thinning of the bones is diagnosed as what (as stated)?
back: Allergic fungal sinusitis.

front: To which lymph nodes does the tip of the tongue drain?
back: The submental lymph nodes.

front: How is local staging of esophageal carcinoma performed?
back: With endoscopic ultrasound.

front: List the causes of superior rib notching.
back: Abnormal osteoblastic activity; osteogenesis imperfecta; connective tissue diseases (rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, Marfan, Sjogren, scleroderma); local pressure; hyperparathyroidism; neurofibromatosis type 1; restrictive lung disease; poliomyelitis; progeria.

front: What causes inferior rib notching (Roesler sign)?
back: Enlarged collateral vessels - coarctation of the aorta, interrupted aortic arch, subclavian artery obstruction, Takayasu disease, Blalock-Taussig shunt (upper two rib spaces only), chest wall AVM, SVC obstruction with venous collaterals, pulmonary AVM, tetralogy of Fallot - and neurogenic tumors (schwannoma, usually single).

front: What is a clay shoveler's fracture and how does it appear on radiographs?
back: A fracture of the spinous process of a lower cervical vertebra (usually C7); an oblique lucency through the spinous process on the lateral view.

front: Which aberrant vessel produces posterior indentation on the esophagus?
back: An aberrant right subclavian artery.

front: Summarise Young's classification of posterior urethral valves.
back: Type 1 - most common: mucosal folds extending anteroinferiorly from the verumontanum and fusing anteriorly; type 2 - rare, no longer considered a valve (normal variant); type 3 - a circular diaphragm with central opening in the membranous urethra below the verumontanum (Cobb collar).

front: What ultrasound criteria define pelvic varices (pelvic congestion)?
back: Venous diameter >=4 mm; flow velocity <=3 cm/s; connection with arcuate vessels in the myometrium; a vein >5 mm traversing the uterine body has ~90% sensitivity.

front: A bleeding duodenal ulcer characteristically erodes which artery?
back: The gastroduodenal artery.

front: On celiac axis angiography (image-based question), which labelled artery was identified?
back: The left gastric artery.

front: When should hysterosalpingography be performed and why?
back: During the proliferative phase (days 6-12), when the endometrium is thinnest - better visualization and minimises the possibility of pregnancy; if pregnancy status is uncertain, beta hCG first.

front: What are the complications of hysterosalpingography?
back: Common but self-limiting: abdominal cramping, vaginal spotting, venous intravasation; rare but serious: pelvic infection, contrast reaction, tubal or uterine perforation.

front: Which radiographic feature supports rheumatic heart disease?
back: Mitral stenosis causing left atrial enlargement.

front: In a child with features of intussusception, which investigation is diagnostic?
back: Abdominal ultrasound.

front: Outline the imaging sequence of a defecography study.
back: Spot lateral images at rest in the left lateral decubitus position; then the seated patient on the defecography chair (right lateral view); optional Kegel (lift) and straining images; finally spot and cine images during evacuation with a post-evacuation straining image.

front: What is the standard lead thickness of a radiation protection apron?
State the 15% rule relating kVp and mAs.
back: When kVp is lowered by 15%, mAs must be doubled; when kVp is increased by 15%, mAs must be multiplied by 0.5 (halved).

front: TOACS Station 1B: A post-trauma radiograph is shown - identify the study and projection.
back: Left knee radiograph, AP projection (L-AP marker).

front: TOACS Station 1B: The frontal knee X-ray shows a lateral tibial plateau fracture - describe its extension and exclude other findings.
back: Intra-articular extension of the lateral tibial plateau fracture; no fracture in the rest of the bones and no joint dislocation.

front: TOACS Station 1B: Lateral tibial plateau fracture with intra-articular extension - what Schatzker type is this?
back: Schatzker type II.

front: TOACS Station 1B: What is the next imaging step for the tibial plateau fracture and the treatment?
back: Next: CT bone window; treatment: open reduction.

front: TOACS Station 2A: Out of the Ten Principles and Ten Commandments of Radiation Protection, write 5.
back: Any 5 of the Ten Principles/Commandments of Radiation Protection (task station).

front: TOACS Station 2B: T1 post-contrast MRI shows multiple brain metastases - whose inclusion criteria do the images match?
back: The NANO-RAD trial.

front: TOACS Station 2B: Describe the MRI findings of the multiple metastases case.
back: Multiple ring-enhancing lesions throughout both cerebral hemispheres, cortical and subcortical, with mild surrounding vasogenic oedema and no mass effect.

front: TOACS Station 3A: Label the radiographic anatomy on a retrograde urethrogram (RGU).
back: Bladder; prostate; membranous urethra; tip of the penis; bulbar urethra; penile urethra.

front: TOACS Station 3B: The MRI shows bilateral ovarian lesions - what was the given diagnosis set?
back: Bilateral ovarian dermoid cysts (in the source TOACS, dermoid cysts were combined with two uterine fibroids).

front: TOACS Station 10A: Describe the Tc-99m generator and identify the displayed curve.
back: The graph is the molybdenum decay curve; 99mTc is supplied in a generator shielded with lead, containing an alumina exchange column on which the parent 99Mo compound is absorbed.

front: TOACS Station 10A: At generator arrival, how does daughter (99mTc) activity compare with parent (99Mo), and how long until equilibrium?
back: Daughter activity has built to its maximum, equal to the parent; it takes approximately four daughter half-lives to reach equilibrium.

front: TOACS Station 10A: After elution, how does 99mTc activity regrow (values at 6 h, 12 h, 24 h)?
back: 50% of the maximum after 6 h, 75% after 12 h, and a new maximum (equilibrium) after 24 h (4 x 6 hours).

front: TOACS Station 4A: What is a CT water bath phantom used for?
back: Used in CT scanning to test uniformity and HU values; for assessing and comparing various image quality indices.

front: TOACS Station 4A: What findings are shown on the CT phantom image?
back: Ring artifact and noise.

front: TOACS Station 4B: A patient presents after strenuous exercise with a chest X-ray - what diagnosis was expected?
back: Pneumomediastinum (the only finding present in this TOACS).

front: TOACS Station 4B: Name the single abnormality shown on this station's chest radiograph.
back: Pneumomediastinum.

front: TOACS Station 5A: For the aortogram station - state the ROI, the effect of decreased cardiac output on contrast, and the arterial sequence timings.
back: ROI for aortogram = descending aorta at the level of the carina; decreased cardiac output delays the contrast bolus (longer time to arrival/peak); arterial sequence: early arterial 15-25 s, late arterial 30-40 s.

front: TOACS Station 5A: The displayed graph is which type of curve?
back: A flow rate curve.

front: How does decreased cardiac output affect the contrast bolus in the aorta?
back: Time to arrival of the bolus and time to peak aortic enhancement increase; peak aortic enhancement increases.

front: Where is the ROI placed for an aortogram?
back: Descending aorta at the level of the carina.

front: State the timing of early and late arterial phases on contrast CT.
back: Early arterial phase 15-25 seconds; late arterial phase 30-40 seconds.

front: TOACS Station 5B: A young patient with hypertension and headache - outline the station's expected answers (technique, findings, diagnosis, next investigation).
back: Technique: MRI abdomen coronal T2WI; findings: innumerable bilateral renal cysts; diagnosis: polycystic kidney disease; next: CT brain angiography for berry aneurysm.

front: TOACS Station 5B: Describe the coronal T2WI MRI findings in the renal cystic station.
back: Innumerable varying-sized cysts, hyperintense on T2WI, in both kidneys.

front: TOACS Station 5B: Innumerable bilateral T2-hyperintense renal cysts on MRI in a young hypertensive - diagnosis?
back: Polycystic kidney disease.

front: TOACS Station 5B: What is the next investigation after diagnosing polycystic kidney disease?
back: CT brain angiography to look for a berry aneurysm.

front: TOACS Station 6A: Label the mammography X-ray unit.
back: X-ray tube; anode; beryllium window; filter; extension cone; compression paddle; grid; cassette; variable position AEC.

front: TOACS Station 6B: Which three questions does this neuro station ask?
back: 1. What is the technique? 2. What are the findings? 3. What is the diagnosis?

front: TOACS Station 6B: Describe the plain CT brain axial findings.
back: Hyperdense area in the left thalamus with intraventricular extension.

front: TOACS Station 6B: Left thalamic hyperdensity with intraventricular extension on plain CT - diagnosis?
back: Left thalamus haemorrhage with interventricular extension.

front: State the focal spot sizes: mammography, magnification mammography, general radiography, fluoroscopy.
back: Mammography 0.3 mm; magnification mammography 0.1 mm; general radiography 1.0-1.2 mm; fluoroscopy 0.6 mm.

front: TOACS Station 7B: Which four questions does the renal mass CT station ask?
back: 1. What is the technique? 2. Findings? 3. Diagnosis? 4. What next?

front: TOACS Station 7B: Describe the CECT abdomen findings in the paediatric renal mass station.
back: Large heterogeneous mass arising from the right kidney, displacing remaining parenchyma anteromedially; mixed solid and cystic areas with only marginal enhancement; no spread into adjacent structures, renal vein or IVC; no nodal or distant metastases in the imaged portions.

front: TOACS Station 7B: A large heterogeneous, marginally enhancing right renal mass in a child - diagnosis?
back: Wilms tumour.

front: TOACS Station 7B: After diagnosing Wilms tumour, what is next?
back: Lung window to see lung metastases; nephrectomy and chemotherapy.

front: TOACS Station 8A: What patient position is used for TRUS-guided prostate biopsy?
back: Left lateral decubitus.

front: TOACS Station 8A: Describe the sextant protocol for prostate sampling.
back: Described by Hodge et al. and later modified: samples are obtained from the peripheral zone (where diagnostic yield is higher) from base through middle to apex of the gland, bilaterally.

front: TOACS Station 8B: In a renal transplant patient's hip imaging station, what must be covered?
back: Findings, diagnosis (bilateral femoral head AVN) and what next.

front: TOACS Station 8B: Describe the T1WI coronal MRI pelvis findings.
back: Bilateral femoral heads show early collapse with subchondral fracture and diffuse sclerosis; the proximal femur shows diffuse oedema.

front: TOACS Station 8B: Bilateral femoral head collapse and sclerosis on MRI after renal transplant - diagnosis?
back: Avascular necrosis (AVN) of both femoral heads.

front: TOACS Station 9A: Where is the ROI placed for CTPA?
back: Below the carina, at the level of the pulmonary trunk - with the ROI on the pulmonary artery.

front: TOACS Station 9B: A patient has fever and abdominal pain with axial and coronal abdominal CTs shown - describe your systematic reading.
back: Technique: CECT abdomen axial and coronal; identify the caecal lesion, fat stranding, lymph nodes, and any hepatic hilar node (see related finding cards).

front: TOACS Station 9B: Describe the CECT abdomen findings.
back: Polypoid mass in the caecum with surrounding fat stranding and locally enlarged lymph nodes; a solitary pathologic lymph node adjacent to the interlobar fissure of the liver.

front: TOACS Station 9B: Polypoid caecal mass with fat stranding and regional nodes on CECT - diagnosis?
back: Ca caecum (caecal carcinoma).

front: TOACS Station 9B: What is next after diagnosing caecal carcinoma on CT?
back: Biopsy and surgery; CECT chest for staging and PET-CT for metastases.

front: TOACS Station 10A: How is the 99mTc generator constructed and shielded?
back: Shielded with lead; contains an alumina exchange column on which a compound of the parent 99Mo is absorbed (displayed graph = molybdenum decay curve).

front: TOACS Station 10A: What is the daughter-to-parent activity relationship at generator arrival and the time to equilibrium?
back: Daughter 99mTc activity has built up to its maximum, equal to the parent 99Mo; equilibrium takes approximately four daughter half-lives.

front: TOACS Station 10A: After elution, what fraction of maximum 99mTc activity is present at 6 h and 12 h, and when is the new maximum?
back: 50% at 6 h; 75% at 12 h; new maximum (equilibrium) after 24 h (4 x 6 hours).

front: List six clinical uses of Tc-99m.
back: 1. Thyroid (trapped but not fully metabolised); 2. gastric emptying studies (mixed with bran porridge); 3. gastric mucosa (Meckel's diverticulum localisation); 4. testicular imaging; 5. salivary glands; 6. cerebral blood flow.

front: What are the uses of molybdenum in imaging?
back: Anode material in some x-ray tubes (especially mammography); filter in mammography; Mo generators as a source of technetium.

front: TOACS Station 10B: A 15-year-old with lower limb pain has a fibula X-ray showing periosteal reaction, partial lysis and cortical interruption - diagnosis?
back: Osteomyelitis.

front: TOACS Station 10B: List the other x-ray findings of osteomyelitis.
back: Regional osteopenia; variable periosteal reaction/thickening (may appear aggressive, including a Codman's triangle); focal bony lysis or cortical loss; endosteal scalloping; loss of trabecular architecture; new bone apposition; eventual peripheral sclerosis.

front: TOACS Station 10B: What features form eventually in chronic or untreated osteomyelitis?
back: A sequestrum, involucrum, and/or cloaca.

front: TOACS Station 10B: What further imaging follows the plain film in osteomyelitis?
back: CECT; scintigraphy; MRI; ultrasound.

front: TOACS Station 11A: Which contrast agents are used in enteroclysis?
back: Barium sulphate and methylcellulose.

front: TOACS Station 11A: Where should the enteroclysis tube tip rest?
back: Second portion of the duodenum for single/double contrast enteroclysis; proximal jejunum if methylcellulose is used.

front: TOACS Station 11A: What are the local uses of enteroclysis?
back: Chronic diarrhea; weight loss; mucosal details; tumour; inflammatory disease.

front: TOACS Station 11B: Describe the scrotal ultrasound findings.
back: Heterogeneous echotexture of the left testis; reactive thickening of the scrotal skin; reactive hydrocele; decreased peripheral testicular flow on colour Doppler; normal right testis.

front: TOACS Station 11B: Heterogeneous left testis with decreased flow and reactive hydrocele - diagnosis?
back: Testicular torsion (left).

front: TOACS Station 12A: A positioning radiograph is presented - which four elements must you identify?
back: The view; the positioning; the centring; the indication.

front: TOACS Station 12A: Describe the positioning for the ankle mortise view.
back: Patient supine or sitting upright with the leg straight; leg internally rotated 15-20 degrees from the hip (intermalleolar line parallel to the detector; 5th toe in line with the centre of the calcaneum); rotation must come from the hip; foot in slight dorsiflexion.

front: TOACS Station 12A: Where is centring for the ankle mortise view and what is the indication?
back: Centring: midpoint of the lateral and medial malleoli; indication: tibial plafond fracture and medial collateral ligament assessment.

front: TOACS Station 12B: What is the given history in this abdominal pain station?
back: Known case of peptic ulcer presenting with abdominal pain.

front: TOACS Station 13A: Which three questions does the Doppler physics station ask?
back: 1. Continuous vs pulsed Doppler; 2. steering angle; 3. Doppler angle and patient position.

front: Describe continuous wave Doppler.
back: Simultaneously transmits and receives with separate piezoelectric crystals; records every velocity along the operator-defined path; captures direction and velocity even at high velocities but cannot localise where individual velocity elements originate.

front: Describe pulsed wave Doppler and its main limitation.
back: The user defines a sample volume (gate) in the B-mode image; based on pulse repetition frequency, only Doppler shifts from that area are recorded; intermittent sampling makes it vulnerable to aliasing at higher velocities, especially farther from the transducer.

front: At what insonation angle is the Doppler signal strongest, and what angle is used in practice?
back: Strongest at 0 degrees (parallel to the vessel); the probe is usually at 30-60 degrees (between 0 and 90 degrees).

front: TOACS Station 13B: Axial temporal bone CT shows a fluid-filled middle ear cavity and diffuse debris in the mastoid air cells - diagnosis?
back: Otomastoiditis.

front: TOACS Station 14A: How is the output of an image intensifier read out?
back: Via fibroptics/lens system; the light output phosphor is read as plumbicon/vidicon.

front: TOACS Station 14B: A smoker with weight loss and fever - CXR shows a deep sulcus sign on the right and a left lower lobe opacity. State the findings.
back: Right-sided deep sulcus sign of pneumothorax; left lower lobe opacity, could be a mass.

front: TOACS Station 15A: Label the neonatal brain ultrasound.
back: Body of lateral ventricle; caudate nucleus; sylvian fissure; thalamus; medulla; interhemispheric fissure; frontal lobe; corpus callosum; septum pellucidum; third ventricle; internal capsule; brainstem (pons); hippocampus.

front: TOACS Station 15B: Fever and cough - HRCT shows multiple tiny branching centrilobular nodules in the right lower lobe. Name the sign.
back: Tree-in-bud appearance.

front: TOACS Station 16A: Label the Towne's view radiograph.
back: Parietal bone; foramen magnum; petrous ridge; posterior clinoid process; lambdoid suture; occipital bone; mastoids; dorsum sellae.

front: TOACS Station 16B: Name the study and the station tasks for this chest case.
back: Study: chest X-ray, PA erect; tasks: name the study, give the findings, give the diagnosis.

front: TOACS Station 16B: Describe the PA chest radiograph findings in the pulmonary hypertension station.
back: Gross enlargement of hila due to pulmonary artery enlargement; peripheral pruning of pulmonary artery branches; moderate cardiomegaly; hiatus hernia.

front: TOACS Station 16B: Enlarged central pulmonary arteries with peripheral pruning and cardiomegaly - diagnosis and differential?
back: Eisenmenger syndrome; differential diagnosis of pulmonary arterial hypertension.

front: TOACS Station 17A: Label the shoulder joint MRI.
back: Supraspinatus and infraspinatus tendons; acromioclavicular joint; acromion; clavicle; trapezius; superior glenoid labrum; suprascapular artery and nerve; humeral head; glenoid; deltoid; inferior glenoid labrum; subscapularis; articular capsule; subscapular artery; posterior circumflex humeral artery; teres major and latissimus dorsi.

front: TOACS Station 17B: A massively enlarged prostate with surrounding inflammation and central liquefaction - diagnosis?
back: Prostatic abscess.

front: TOACS Station 17B: What is the next step in prostatic abscess?
back: MRI; drainage of the abscess; antibiotic cover; PSA levels.

front: TOACS Station 18A: Three hip radiographs (A, B, C) are presented side by side - what is being tested?
back: Recognition of hip positioning/rotation across the three radiographs (see the related positioning card).

front: TOACS Station 18A: The three hips show eversion (A), neutral (B) and inversion (C) - which position is best?
back: B - the neutral position.

front: TOACS Station 18B: Label the fallopian tube on HSG.
back: Interstitial part; isthmus part; ampulla part - with full demonstration of the fallopian tube.

front: TOACS Station 18B: Which HSG findings indicate a normal study?
back: Free intraperitoneal spillage of contrast and convexity of the uterine fundus.

front: TOACS Station 19A: A child with headache has partial opacification of both maxillary sinuses with air-fluid levels - what does this indicate?
back: Bilateral maxillary sinusitis with air-fluid levels (acute inflammatory fluid).

front: TOACS Station 19A: How is the rest of the paranasal sinus study reported?
back: Right frontal sinus is not pneumatised; the other paranasal sinuses are unremarkable; nasal septum normal.

front: TOACS Station 19B: Describe the findings in the obstructive jaundice MRCP station.
back: Dilated CBD with multiple signal voids in its mid and lower portions; mild intrahepatic biliary dilatation.

front: TOACS Station 19B: A dilated CBD with multiple signal voids on MRCP - diagnosis?
back: Choledocholithiasis.

front: TOACS Station 20A: Label the barium meal radiograph.
back: Fundus of stomach; duodenum first part; duodenum second part; body; pylorus; angular notch; pyloric antrum; jejunum.

front: TOACS Station 20B: Describe the MLO and CC mammogram findings.
back: Well-defined lobulated high-density lesion with fine spiculations in the lower inner quadrant of the right breast; no parenchymal distortion, pleomorphic microcalcification clusters, skin thickening, nipple retraction or significant axillary lymphadenopathy.

front: TOACS Station 20B: A lobulated high-density mass with fine spiculation in the right breast - what BI-RADS category?
back: BI-RADS 4.

front: TOACS Station 20B: What is the next step for this BI-RADS 4 breast lesion?
back: Ultrasound and ultrasound-guided core biopsy.

front: TOACS Station 20B: How is the left breast reported?
back: No suspicious abnormality seen.

front: What is the classic appearance of ascitic fluid in tuberculous peritonitis?
back: Straw-coloured, lymphocyte-predominant exudate (NB: cirrhotic ascites can also be straw-coloured - discriminators are lymphocytic exudate/SAAG/ADA). Paper key said 'inflammatory' (hedged with '??') - DISPUTED, not KEY WRONG.

front: After barium aspiration during a swallow study, what treatment is recommended?
back: Chest physiotherapy to promote clearance (Radiopaedia: 'the only treatment recommended'); tiny microaspiration may be asymptomatic; BAL is not routine.

front: Suspected ovarian cancer (large complex adnexal mass, raised CA-125): what is the staging step, and who decides between primary debulking and neoadjuvant chemotherapy?
back: Contrast-enhanced CT chest/abdomen/pelvis; the choice of primary debulking surgery vs biopsy + neoadjuvant chemotherapy is made in a specialist (MDT) centre (ESMO-ESGO 2019). The Feb 2025 paper's Q13 key conflicts with its own annotation - see disputed.md.

front: Unruptured ectopic pregnancy: what is the characteristic ultrasound finding?
back: An adnexal mass with an echogenic tubal ring (bagel / tubal ring sign).

front: Mammography: a lesion that is higher on the true lateral (ML) view than on the MLO view lies where?
back: Medially - 'muffins rise, lead falls' (medial lesions rise, lateral lesions fall).

front: Conventional tomography: how does the swing angle relate to section thickness?
back: Wider angle = thinner section; narrower angle = thicker section.

front: Which CT generation underlies modern scanners, and what limits the 4th generation?
back: Third generation (rotate-rotate). Fourth generation (rotate-stationary, fixed detector ring) cannot use in-plane anti-scatter collimation and is costlier.

front: What does scatter radiation do to the radiographic image?
back: Increases fog and reduces radiographic contrast.

front: Which component of the x-ray circuit selects kVp, and what does it feed?
back: The autotransformer (kVp selector); it supplies the step-up transformer, which provides the tube high voltage.

front: Tungsten K-edge energy?
back: About 69.5 keV (NIST XCOM: 6.95250E-02 MeV).

front: What share of a diagnostic x-ray beam is bremsstrahlung (tungsten target)?
back: 100% below ~70 kVp, about 85% above 70 kVp (Radiology Key); the Feb 2025 paper states 90%. Not the same as the ~1% of electron energy that becomes x-rays (99% heat).

front: State the 15% rule in radiography.
back: Changing kVp by 15% has the same effect on receptor exposure as doubling (or halving) the mAs.

front: Characteristic x-ray energies of a molybdenum anode in mammography?
back: 17.5 and 19.6 keV, close to the ~20 keV optimum for breast imaging.
