front: Unenhanced CT: what liver attenuation suggests hepatic steatosis?
back: Absolute liver attenuation below 40 HU (or liver lower than spleen).

front: Most common variant of the right hepatic artery (Michels)?
back: Replaced RHA from the SMA (Michels type 3), ~10% (range 8-11%).

front: Dose range measurable with TLDs?
back: 0.01 mGy to 10 Gy.

front: Step-up transformer: turns ratio and effect on voltage and current?
back: More turns on the secondary than the primary: voltage up, current down.

front: Annual occupational dose limit for a radiation worker (name both editions)?
back: US NRC: 50 mSv/yr (5 rem = 5000 mrem). ICRP: 20 mSv/yr averaged over 5 years, no single year above 50 mSv. 1 rem = 10 mSv; 1 mSv = 100 mrem.

front: Gadolinium contrast and breastfeeding: how much reaches the milk and the infant, and what is advised?
back: <0.04% of the administered dose is secreted into milk; <0.0004% of the maternal dose is absorbed by the infant; guidelines do not support stopping breastfeeding. (The source paper's 'about 0.5%' is too high.)

front: Effective dose: PA chest x-ray vs CT chest?
back: PA chest x-ray ~0.02 mSv; CT chest ~6-8 mSv (the paper's 2 mSv is too low).

front: What controls slice thickness in MRI?
back: The slope of the slice-select gradient together with the transmit RF bandwidth (steep gradient + narrow bandwidth = thin slice).

front: Rank effective dose (CT, Tc-99m bone scan, plain x-ray) with typical values.
back: CT > bone scan > x-ray. CT chest ~6-8 mSv (abdomen/pelvis ~7.7); bone scan ~3-4 mSv; chest radiograph ~0.02-0.1 mSv. (The paper's 20/15/1 mSv are inflated.)

front: How is motion artifact reduced in a child with a forearm fracture?
back: Short exposure time, immobilisation aids and parental presence/involvement.

front: CAVITY mnemonic for cavitating lung lesions?
back: Cancer (SCC, cavitary mets); Autoimmune (GPA, rheumatoid nodules); Vascular (bland/septic emboli); Infection (abscess, TB); Trauma (pneumatocele); Youth (CPAM; also sequestration, bronchogenic cyst).

front: Causes of multiple filling defects of the ureter - and which listed condition is NOT a cause?
back: Multifocal urothelial carcinoma, vascular indentations, multiple stones (steinstrasse), clots, ureteritis cystica, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, malacoplakia, leukoplakia. Aplastic anaemia is not a cause.

front: Causes of vertebral body squaring?
back: Ankylosing spondylitis is the most common cause; uncommon: Paget disease and inflammatory arthritides (rheumatoid, reactive, psoriatic, juvenile idiopathic); Down syndrome and block vertebra also listed. Flowing ossification = DISH. The source paper's answer 'psoriatic' is on the list but uncommon.

front: Pathologic lead points in childhood intussusception: frequency and commonest types?
back: About 6% of cases; commonest benign = Meckel diverticulum, commonest malignant = lymphoma; also duplication cysts and polyps.

front: Kuhl breast MRI kinetic curves?
back: Type I persistent - usually benign (~9% of malignant lesions); II plateau - concerning; III washout - strongly suggestive of malignancy.

front: Chemical-shift MRI for adrenal adenoma: the signal-drop threshold?
back: Opposed-phase signal drop >16.5% indicates adenoma (published thresholds 16.5-20%).

front: Adrenal mass of 10-30 HU: accuracy of out-of-phase MRI for adenoma?
back: Sensitivity 89%, specificity 100% (10-20 HU: 100%/100%) (AJR 2005).

front: Which mediastinal compartment holds the descending thoracic aorta? (name the classification)
back: Classical anterior/middle/posterior division: posterior mediastinum. ITMIG classification: visceral (middle) compartment.

front: Defecography (evacuation proctography) technique?
back: Rectum opacified with thick barium paste via catheter; vagina (and small bowel, for enterocele) may be opacified; patient seated on a commode, evacuation imaged in lateral projection.

front: Where do tracheal diverticula arise?
back: 97% at the right posterolateral trachea near the thoracic inlet.

front: Technique-chart rule for patient thickness?
back: Double the exposure (mAs/time) for every ~4 cm increase in patient thickness (one study: 3.5 cm is more exact).

front: Define quality assurance in diagnostic radiology.
back: Systematic actions that ensure consistently high-quality images with minimum exposure of patients and staff.

front: CTPA bolus tracking: ROI and trigger?
back: ROI on the pulmonary artery below the carina (pulmonary trunk level); trigger ~100 HU (protocols 80-100 HU).

front: Contraindications to barium enema?
back: Suspected colonic perforation, toxic megacolon, pseudomembranous colitis.

front: Testicular torsion: definitive next step?
back: Urgent surgical exploration with detorsion; orchiopexy if viable (fix the contralateral testis too); orchiectomy only if non-viable.

front: Doppler angle correction limits?
back: Keep the angle at or below 60 degrees; above 60 degrees velocity errors of up to 20-30% occur; keep the angle constant for serial studies.

front: How many stages of haematoma evolution are recognised and what is the T2 signal in the acute stage?
back: Intracranial haematoma evolution on MRI is described in five stages; in the acute stage the T2 signal intensity drops (T2 shortening) and the haematoma becomes hypointense.

front: TLD badge worn under vs outside the lead apron: what does each reflect?
back: A TLD badge worn under the lead apron reflects body dose; worn outside the apron it reflects extremity/thyroid dose.

front: Why is the AP erect chest view often chosen in younger children?
back: Paediatric chest radiography: in younger children an AP erect projection is typically easier to obtain than a PA projection.

front: V/Q ventilation scan: technique and imaging phases?
back: V/Q ventilation scan: Tc-99m DTPA aerosol is inhaled through a non-rebreathing mask with the patient supine; the micro-aerosol particles reach the distal tracheobronchial tree and reflect regional ventilation; imaging is upright in three phases - initial breath, equilibrium and washout.

front: V/Q perfusion scan: agent, particle site and camera?
back: V/Q perfusion scan: Tc-99m MAA is injected intravenously with the patient supine; the MAA particles lodge in pre-capillary arterioles; a high-resolution large-field-of-view gamma camera images the lungs.

front: What has replaced double-contrast barium enema for colon cancer screening?
back: Double-contrast barium enema was used for colon cancer (polyp) screening and for follow-up of failed colonoscopy; CT colonography has effectively replaced it.

front: Indications for CT colonography?
back: CT colonography (virtual colonoscopy, CT pneumocolon) is a minimally invasive technique indicated for colorectal cancer screening, after incomplete or unsuccessful optical colonoscopy, for assessment of strictures, and to evaluate the colon proximal to an obstructing neoplasm.

front: CT colonography preparation, distension and antispasmodic?
back: CT colonography technique: the colon must be clean and completely distended (residual stool or fluid gives false results); IV contrast is not necessary for colonic interpretation; hyoscine-N-butylbromide (Buscopan) reduces motion and discomfort, while IV glucagon is used in some centres but its efficacy is contentious.

front: Absolute and relative contraindications to CT colonography?
back: CT colonography contraindications: absolute - acute inflammatory conditions (acute diverticulitis, active ulcerative colitis or Crohn disease) and recent abdominal or pelvic surgery; relative - pregnancy, claustrophobia and severe contrast reaction/anaphylaxis (barium protocols are an alternative).

front: Virtual colonoscopy advantages and disadvantages versus optical colonoscopy?
back: Virtual vs optical colonoscopy: virtual colonoscopy is less invasive with fewer complications, is quicker, can image beyond an obstruction and shows extracolonic pathology; but residual faeces can mislead, no biopsy can be taken and it uses ionising radiation.

front: Iodinated contrast and breastfeeding: half-life, milk excretion and advice?
back: Iodinated contrast: plasma half-life about 2 hours with ~100% excreted in 24 hours; less than 1% of the dose enters breast milk (poor lipid solubility); an allergic reaction from milk is theoretical and has never been reported; if the mother remains concerned, expressing and discarding milk for 12-24 hours is a conservative option, with no benefit beyond 24 hours.

front: Gadolinium contrast: half-life, chelation and the conservative breastfeeding option?
back: Gadolinium agents: plasma half-life about 2 hours with ~100% excreted in 24 hours; any gadolinium in milk is thought to be in a stable chelated form; expressing and discarding milk for 12-24 hours is offered only if the mother remains concerned.

front: Causes of a short metacarpal?
back: Causes of a short metacarpal: post-traumatic (growth-plate injury) is common; uncommon causes include Gorlin (basal cell naevus) syndrome, hereditary multiple exostoses, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, sickle cell disease with infarction, homocystinuria and Langer-Giedion syndrome; isolated short 5th metacarpals are described in a familial type 1 diabetes variant.

front: Carotid Doppler PSV threshold for severe ICA stenosis?
back: Carotid Doppler: the further the Doppler parameters lie above the PSV threshold of 230 cm/s, the greater the likelihood of severe disease.

front: Near occlusion vs total occlusion of the ICA on ultrasound?
back: Near occlusion of the ICA has variable velocity parameters (high, low or undetectable) and is diagnosed by a markedly narrowed lumen with trickle flow on colour/power Doppler; total ICA occlusion shows no luminal patency on grey-scale and no flow on colour, spectral or power Doppler, and the contralateral carotid may show compensatory increased velocity.

front: Define intra-axial and extra-axial lesions and how they behave.
back: Intra-axial lesions arise within the brain parenchyma (a mass is intra-axial if completely surrounded by parenchyma); extra-axial lesions arise outside the parenchyma within the cranial cavity (meninges, CSF spaces).

front: Commonest primaries presenting with pulmonary metastases in adults?
back: In middle-aged and older adults the commonest malignancies presenting with pulmonary metastases are lung, colorectal, renal cell, pancreatic and breast cancer.

front: Contents of the carpal tunnel from superficial to deep?
back: Carpal tunnel contents from superficial to deep: four flexor digitorum superficialis tendons (middle and ring finger tendons more superficial than index and little), the median nerve, the flexor pollicis longus tendon (lateral, own synovial sheath) and four flexor digitorum profundus tendons (FDS and FDP share one sheath); flexor carpi radialis is wrongly said to lie in the tunnel.

front: Where do flexor carpi radialis and palmaris longus lie relative to the flexor retinaculum?
back: Flexor carpi radialis runs between the layers of the flexor retinaculum in its own compartment, and the palmaris longus is attached to the superficial surface of the flexor retinaculum.

front: Causes of pulmonary calcification?
back: Causes of pulmonary calcification: healed varicella pneumonia, pneumoconioses (silicosis, coal worker's, stannosis, baritosis), mitral stenosis, pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis, amyloidosis (amorphous), metastatic calcification (end-stage renal disease, after solid-organ transplant) and pulmonary arterial calcification; calcified nodules or masses occur with hyalinising granuloma, hamartoma, chondroma, calcifying fibrous pseudotumour and calcifying metastases.

front: Can CPR cause posterior rib fractures in a child?
back: Posterior rib fractures do not occur from CPR (vigorous CPR can occasionally cause anterior rib fractures), so posterior rib fractures in a child point away from CPR.

front: Which skull and long-bone fractures are more or less specific for non-accidental injury?
back: Skull fractures in non-accidental injury: non-parietal, multi-bone (complex), sutural diastasis and depressed fractures are moderately specific; simple linear parietal fractures have low specificity (favouring accidental injury); single diaphyseal fractures have low specificity (spiral humeral fracture is an exception).

front: Where does ischaemic colitis occur in low-flow states versus vessel occlusion?
back: Ischaemic colitis location follows mesenteric vessel anatomy: low-flow states and non-occlusive disease are the commonest causes and affect the watershed areas, whereas complete occlusion (e.g. acute SMA occlusion) involves the whole vascular territory.

front: Indications and contraindication of evacuation proctography?
back: Evacuation proctography (defecography) is a fluoroscopic (or MR) technique to evaluate pelvic floor prolapse; indications are incomplete or obstructed defecation/constipation, pelvic floor disorder, rectal prolapse and faecal incontinence; a postoperative rectum (e.g. coloanal anastomosis) is a contraindication or needs caution before loading and stressing it.

front: Defecography: commode, barium consistency and filling endpoint?
back: Defecography technique: a special commode on the fluoroscopy table; barium may be mixed with breadcrumbs, cornflour or porridge powder to give a stool-like consistency; rectal filling stops when the patient has an urge to defecate; optional cine/spot images are taken while straining without defecating; the patient needs privacy.

front: Define the anorectal angle and what changes during normal evacuation?
back: The anorectal angle is formed by a line parallel to the anal canal and a line parallel to the posterior rectum; its change reflects puborectalis strength; the pelvic floor normally descends a few centimetres on straining, and during normal evacuation the puborectalis impression on the distal posterior rectal wall is lost.

front: SCFE: why are both hips imaged?
back: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis: AP and frog-leg pelvis views are done bilaterally because many cases are bilateral and the normal side provides comparison.

front: Aetiology and age pattern of idiopathic childhood intussusception?
back: Childhood intussusception is relatively rare in the first three months of life (passive immunity); idiopathic cases are thought to relate to hypertrophic lymphoid tissue (Peyer patches) following an infection.

front: Chemical shift MRI of an adrenal mass: findings and pitfalls?
back: Chemical shift MRI is the most reliable imaging for adrenal adenoma when CT is equivocal: intracellular fat gives signal loss on opposed-phase images, a visible loss of signal comparing in- and out-of-phase images (same windowing) is diagnostic, the liver should not be used as the reference (steatosis, haemochromatosis), and sensitivity and specificity depend on the lesion's CT density.

front: Which adrenal metastases can mimic an adenoma on chemical shift MRI?
back: Fat-containing adrenal metastases (hepatocellular carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma) can lose signal on out-of-phase imaging like adenomas; malignant adrenal lesions also show restricted diffusion.

front: Boundaries of the pyriform sinus?
back: The pyriform sinus is bounded medially by the aryepiglottic fold and the arytenoid and cricoid cartilages, superiorly by the level of the hyoid bone and inferiorly by the lower border of the cricoid cartilage.

front: Territory of the recurrent artery of Heubner?
back: The recurrent artery of Heubner supplies the head of the caudate, the medial globus pallidus and the anterior limb of the internal capsule, plus the anterior hypothalamus, nucleus accumbens, parts of the uncinate fasciculus, diagonal band of Broca and basal nucleus of Meynert.

front: Rib notching: single vs multiple causes and the NF1 pattern?
back: Rib notching may affect a single rib (trauma, solitary mass such as schwannoma) or multiple ribs; in neurofibromatosis type 1 the notching is usually inferior but can rarely be superior when the neurofibroma is very large.

front: Chest radiograph assessment of a thoracic aortic aneurysm: limits and mimics?
back: Thoracic aortic aneurysms are usually visible on frontal and lateral chest radiographs, but size is hard to assess because of magnification and poor visualisation; mediastinal masses can mimic them and mural calcification occurs in atherosclerosis and aortitis.

front: How do clay-shoveler fractures present and when are they found?
back: Clay-shoveler fractures are often unrecognised at the time and found incidentally years later; acute cases are associated with motor vehicle accidents, sudden muscle contraction and direct blows.

front: HSG: indications, contraindications and timing?
back: HSG is a fluoroscopic study of the uterus and fallopian tubes used mainly for infertility (uterine morphology, tubal patency) or recurrent abortion; contraindications are pregnancy, active pelvic infection, recent uterine/tubal surgery and contrast allergy; it is performed in the proliferative phase for best visualisation and least chance of pregnancy.

front: HSG catheters, pitfalls and false-positive tubal block?
back: HSG technique: speculum in lithotomy position after antiseptic cleaning; catheter options are a 6 Fr balloon Foley (difficult in an angulated cervix; place just beyond the internal os), an HSG catheter or metal acorn-tipped cannula (Leech Wilkinson allows tubal clearance; Margolin has a silicone tip for a narrow cervix); a tenaculum gives traction; prime the device with contrast to avoid bubbles that mimic filling defects; an inadequate balloon seal causes leakage and a false-positive tubal block.

front: HSG contrast and standard images?
back: HSG contrast: water-soluble iodinated contrast is injected slowly under fluoroscopy; Lipiodol is used by some for infertility (increased fertility reported but debated); a typical study has a preliminary pelvis view then spot images of the endometrial contour, filled tubes and bilateral intraperitoneal spill.

front: Uterine and tubal abnormalities seen on HSG?
back: HSG findings: uterine - congenital anomalies, submucosal fibroids, malignancy, adenomyosis, adhesions, polyps; tubal - obliteration (usually from previous pelvic inflammation; differentiate from spasm or underfilling), polyps, malignancy, hydrosalpinx and salpingitis isthmica nodosa; tubal spasm can be physiological.

front: Image intensifier: electrodes and the conversion chain?
back: Image intensifier: the input fluorescent screen converts X-rays to light photons, the photocathode converts these to photoelectrons, and an electric field between the photocathode and the anode accelerates them to the output screen.

front: Factors that increase scatter and how to reduce it?
back: Scatter radiation increases with tissue volume (thickness), tube kilovoltage and field size, and close collimation reduces it.

front: How do stiffness and density affect ultrasound velocity?
back: Ultrasound velocity is higher in stiffer (less compressible) and less dense materials.

front: Distribution of pleural plaques?
back: Pleural plaques spare the apices and costophrenic angles, frequently arise from the mediastinal pleura and only infrequently involve the visceral pleura.

front: Next step for a BI-RADS 4 lesion?
back: BI-RADS 4 (suspicious) breast lesion: biopsy (tissue diagnosis) is the next step.

front: Name the basal cisterns.
back: Basal cisterns: suprasellar, lamina terminalis, Sylvian, crural, interpeduncular, ambient and quadrigeminal.

front: Parts of the temporal bone and the cochlear promontory?
back: The temporal bone has squamous, mastoid, petrous and tympanic parts plus the styloid process.

front: Segments of the facial nerve on temporal bone CT?
back: Facial nerve segments on CT temporal bone: labyrinthine, geniculate ganglion, tympanic and mastoid.

front: Mo-99 and Tc-99m half-lives and the generator equilibrium?
back: Mo-99 (half-life 65.9 h; the station states 67 h) decays to Tc-99m (half-life 6.0 h).

front: Next investigation for ADPKD with hypertension and headache?
back: ADPKD with hypertension and headache: investigate with CT or MR angiography of the brain for an intracranial (berry) aneurysm.

front: What is grid frequency also called?
back: Grid frequency is also known as strip line density (lead strips per unit length).

front: Which less common conditions can act as lead points of intussusception?
back: Metastases (malignant melanoma, breast and lung cancer), mural haematoma from trauma and intestinal polyps can act as lead points of intussusception.
